echoes.note: The healed man 'walking, leaping' (vv. 8-9) enacts Isaiah's eschatological promise 'then shall the lame man leap as a hart'; the verbal pairing of lameness and leaping is the signature image, and Luke uses the same scene to frame the apostolic age as the dawning restoration of Israel.

Same oracle of bodily restoration in the messianic age ('eyes of the blind opened'); the lame-man healing as a sign of the new era partakes of the wider Isa 35 catalogue even though only the lameness clause (v. 6) is verbally activated.
'He raiseth up the poor out of the dust' resonates faintly with the beggar at the gate being raised up; thematic coherence with God lifting the destitute, but no verbal borrowing.

'The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers' (v. 13) reproduces the patriarchal covenant formula of the burning bush, anchoring the resurrection proclamation in the God who self-identifies to Moses.

The expanded title 'the God of our fathers' as the LORD's memorial name reinforces the Exodus 3 self-disclosure; v. 15 supplies the 'God of your fathers... my name for ever' phrasing behind Peter's formula.

'has glorified his Servant (pais) Jesus' (v. 13) echoes the LXX of the fourth Servant Song, 'my servant... shall be exalted and glorified'; the combination of pais + glorification is a deliberate Servant identification.
The 'Righteous One' (v. 14) whom they denied draws on the suffering Servant who is called 'the righteous one, my servant' who justifies many; coheres with the pais/Servant frame of v. 13.

'the Holy One' (v. 14) recalls the Davidic 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' cited fully in Acts 2:27; the title clusters here with the resurrection claim 'God raised from the dead' (v. 15).
'whom you delivered up' (v. 13) faintly mirrors the Servant who 'was delivered up' (paredothe) for the transgressors; the handing-over language belongs to the same Servant matrix.

'you did this in ignorance' (v. 17) invokes the Torah distinction between unwitting sin (atonable) and high-handed sin; Peter casts the crucifixion as forgivable ignorance, opening the call to repentance.
The priestly category of sinning 'through ignorance' underlies Peter's exoneration in v. 17; thematic, no verbal quotation.
'that your sins may be blotted out' (v. 19) echoes the LORD's promise 'I am he that blotteth out thy transgressions'; the blotting-out image of divine forgiveness is distinctive.
'blot out my transgressions' supplies the same penitential idiom behind v. 19; coheres with the call to repent, though Isa 43 is the closer match.

'times of restoration (apokatastasis) of all things' (v. 21) draws on the Elijah-tradition of restoring/turning hearts before the day of the LORD; LXX Mal 3:23-24 uses apokatastesei, the verbal root behind Peter's eschatological 'restoration'.
Joel's promise of God restoring the years coheres with the 'times of refreshing... restoration of all things' (vv. 19-21); thematic restoration motif, no verbal link.

vv. 22-23 quote the promise of 'a prophet like me from among your brethren... you shall listen to him,' applied to Jesus as the eschatological prophet-like-Moses; the most explicit OT citation in the sermon.

The penalty clause 'every soul that will not listen... shall be utterly destroyed from among the people' (v. 23) is not in Deut 18 but fused from Lev 23:29 ('cut off from his people'); a conflated citation, classic of the Acts speeches.
'In your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed' (v. 25) cites the Abrahamic promise after the Aqedah, grounding the gospel's reach to all nations in the patriarchal covenant.

The base form of the blessing-to-the-families promise; Peter's 'all the families of the earth' matches Gen 12:3 ('families') more closely than the 'nations' of Gen 22:18, so both stand behind the citation.
'the covenant which God made with our fathers' (v. 25) recalls the everlasting covenant established with Abraham and his seed; supplies the covenantal frame for the quoted blessing.

'turning away every one of you from your wickedness' (v. 26) faintly echoes 'the Redeemer shall come... unto them that turn from transgression in Jacob'; thematic turning-from-sin, no firm verbal tie.
'all the prophets from Samuel' (v. 24) presupposes Samuel's establishment as the LORD's prophet to all Israel; an allusive nod to the prophetic line's inauguration rather than a quotation.
